passage: I'm Elizabeth, and I sit two desks from Yash. For months I've noticed him turning his phone face down whenever it buzzes. Last Friday he skipped lunch, and I glimpsed his screen before he tilted it away: he seemed to be paying one card's bill with cash drawn from another. His parents keep asking when he will visit, and he keeps saying work is heavy. Once he muttered, "If I clear this one first, then I'll tell them." I don't know for sure what's going on; maybe it's nothing. I asked him for tea and said quietly that if money is ever tight, talking early gives more choices than waiting. He looked into his cup. "Maybe next week."

qa.q: Where does Elizabeth sit in relation to Yash at work?
qa.a: Elizabeth sits two desks from Yash.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth say "maybe it's nothing" even after glimpsing the screen?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt concerned but uncertain, and knew that a glimpse of a screen does not prove what is really going on.

qa.q: What could Yash do to keep more options open?
qa.a: Yash could talk early to someone he trusts, such as his parents, and work out a repayment plan before the debt grows.

qa.q: What might it be like for Yash to keep telling his parents that work is heavy?
qa.a: Lonely and anxious, since Yash carries the worry alone and keeps putting off the conversation with his family.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's eyes, someone paying one card with another and hiding it from family while shame delays talking.

passage:
Day 1. Sabina paid the minimum on her second card with cash drawn from her first, then answered her mother's weekly call with "All fine, Amma." Her stomach was tight as Usha talked about a neighbour's wedding.

Day 12. Reminder messages piled up. She skipped a cousin's dinner so nobody could ask, and lay awake doing sums on the back of an envelope.

Day 20. On a walk with her mother she said it in one breath: three cards, none paid off. Usha stopped, was quiet, then said, "Show me the numbers." They wrote each amount and date on one page. The next morning Sabina phoned the card company and asked what repayment plan they could offer.

qa.q: What did Sabina do on Day 12 so nobody could ask her questions?
qa.a: She skipped a cousin's dinner.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling on the night she lay awake doing sums?
qa.a: Anxious and ashamed, since reminders kept piling up and she was hiding the debt from her family.

qa.q: What did Sabina do on Day 20 that left her with more options?
qa.a: She told her mother about the three cards, wrote each amount and date on one page, and next morning phoned the card company about a repayment plan.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Sabina finally told her?
qa.a: Usha was probably surprised and worried but calm and supportive, since Usha stopped, stayed quiet, and asked to see the numbers.

grounding: Shows someone juggling cards in secret, with anxiety growing until honesty and a repayment plan open options.

passage:
Dear Mohit,
I have started this letter four times. Here is the truth. For eight months I have been paying one credit card with the other. When the second card filled up, I took a small personal loan to pay it. Every month I tell Amma everything is fine, and every month the number is bigger.
I stopped opening the bank envelopes. I sleep badly. Last week you asked why I skipped your birthday dinner, and I said work. It was not work. I could not face paying for anyone's meal.
I am telling you first because you won't panic. I have made a list of every card, loan and due date. On Saturday I want to go to the bank and ask about a repayment plan, and I want you to come. After that, we tell Amma together.
Your brother,
Pankaj

qa.q: How long has Pankaj been paying one credit card with the other?
qa.a: Pankaj has been paying one credit card with the other for eight months.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj stop opening the bank envelopes?
qa.a: Pankaj was anxious and ashamed of the growing number, so avoiding the envelopes felt easier than facing it.

qa.q: What could make Pankaj's Saturday visit to the bank more useful?
qa.a: Taking the list of every card, loan and due date and asking the bank to explain the options for a repayment plan, with Mohit there for support.

qa.q: What might Mohit feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Mohit may feel shocked and sad that his brother hid it so long, but also trusted, since Pankaj told Mohit first and asked for help.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult covering one debt with another, hiding growing anxiety from family, and choosing to speak up and plan repayment.

passage:
Hemant, you've known me since school, and you know Uday was always the one who paid for chai. That was part of the problem. Last year I had two cards and a personal loan, and I was using each one to pay the next. My wife thought the bonus had cleared everything. I let her think that.
Every time my phone buzzed I thought it was the bank. I stopped answering unknown numbers. I snapped at my son over homework. It wasn't homework I was angry at.
What changed? One night I just said it at dinner. My wife was quiet for a long time, then she said, "Why didn't you tell me when it was small?" We went to the bank together and they set up a plan with fixed dates. A counsellor there explained which loan to close first. It's still not done. But I sleep now, yaar. I wish I had spoken a year earlier.

qa.q: What did Uday's wife think had cleared everything?
qa.a: Uday's wife thought the bonus had cleared everything.

qa.q: Why did Uday stop answering unknown numbers?
qa.a: Uday was anxious and dreaded calls from the bank, and the fear made Uday avoid anything that might be about the debt.

qa.q: Which choice turned things around for Uday, and why?
qa.a: Telling his wife at dinner and going to the bank together turned it around, because honesty opened the door to a fixed plan and advice from a counsellor.

qa.q: How did Uday's wife feel when she heard the truth?
qa.a: She was quiet for a long time and seemed hurt, asking why he had not told her when it was small.

grounding: Shows a man caught paying debts with debts who hides it from his wife until honesty and a bank repayment plan ease the pressure.

passage:
March. Jomon moved the card statement from the table to his bag before his sister Rehana came home. He paid the minimum on one card using the other, then opened a third card offer "just for a month." He told himself it was temporary.
April. He woke at 3 a.m. two nights running, adding numbers in his head. At work he typed the wrong figure in an invoice. When Rehana asked if he was all right, he said, "Tired, that's all." That Sunday she found the statement fallen behind the sofa.
May. They sat at the dining table with a notebook. Jomon wrote every card, every balance and every date. Rehana did not lecture; she just asked, "Which bank do we call first?" On Monday he met a debt counsellor at his bank. By the end of May he had closed the third card and was paying on one plan with one date.

qa.q: Where did Rehana find the statement?
qa.a: Rehana found the statement fallen behind the sofa.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling in April, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Jomon was anxious and stressed; he woke at 3 a.m. adding numbers and made a mistake in an invoice.

qa.q: What small step in May made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Writing every card, balance and date in one notebook with Rehana made the debt visible and let him take it to a debt counsellor.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when she finds the statement?
qa.a: Rehana may feel worried and a little hurt that Jomon hid it, but she chooses to help calmly instead of lecturing.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult sinking deeper by covering one card with another, hiding it from family, then choosing honesty and one repayment plan.

passage: "Vasudha, I saw you slip that bank envelope into your drawer. I won't ask. Just let old Divyansh from accounts tell you about my twenty-fifth year. I had two credit cards, and when the first bill came, I paid it with the second. Then the second with the first. Every month the hole got deeper and the story got neater. I stopped opening envelopes. I told my wife, Meera, that the bank had made an error. I slept badly, snapped at everyone and jumped whenever the landline rang. One night she found a statement in my scooter box. I expected shouting. She sat down and said, 'How long have you been carrying this alone?' The next week we went to the bank together and asked for a repayment plan. It took three years. If I had spoken in the second month instead of the fourteenth, it would have taken far less."

qa.q: Where did Meera find the statement?
qa.a: In Divyansh's scooter box.

qa.q: What was young Divyansh feeling while hiding the cards?
qa.a: Young Divyansh was anxious and ashamed, sleeping badly, snapping at everyone and jumping at every phone call.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Divyansh's story?
qa.a: Meera finding the statement and asking how long Divyansh had carried it alone, after which they went to the bank together and asked for a repayment plan.

qa.q: How might Meera have felt when she found the statement?
qa.a: Meera was probably hurt by the hiding, but her first reaction was concern, not anger.

grounding: Shows a young earner paying one card with another, growing anxious and hiding it from a spouse until honesty and a repayment plan open a way out.
